character_and_relationship_context:
Aminata Diallo rises before dawn each day, the only light in her rented room a thin glow of a kerosene lamp. She lives in a bustling district on the outskirts of Bamako, where the walls are packed earth and the roof corrugated tin. She fills a bucket each morning at the communal stand two blocks away and carries it back with a careful gait to avoid splashing her only pair of work trousers. She wears the trousers six days a week to the construction site, where she is the youngest person on the crew and the only woman. Her master mason, Sékou, who lost two fingers to a faulty crane, calls her la petite comptable because she recalculates every load-bearing estimate in her head before she lifts a trowel. She does not laugh at his teasing; she simply nods and checks the angle of the plumb line again. Double-checking is a reflex born from watching her mother lose a market stall to a miscalculated loan. Aminata was twelve when her mother died, and she has been counting everything ever since: the number of bricks in a pallet, the cost of a bag of rice, the weeks until her next accounting exam. She keeps a small notebook tucked inside her shirt, filled with figures and dates, and under the loosest floorboard near her mattress she hides an emergency fund—exactly the same amount each month, never touched, never counted in daylight. At night, after ten hours of hauling cement and stacking blocks, she studies by the lamp until her eyes burn. The accounting course she is saving for meets at a community center on the other side of the city, but she cannot afford the bus fare both ways, so she walks. She walks past the stalls of women selling fried plantains, past the boys who whistle and call her mademoiselle bâtisseuse, and she keeps her eyes on the ground, counting her steps. She is saving for something else too, something she does not write in her notebook: a proper room with running water, where her younger sister can come live with her and go to school. But she does not speak of this aloud, because in her experience, plans that are spoken become plans that are borrowed against. Her coworkers respect her silence, her precision, the way she never asks for an advance on her wage. They do not know that she once watched her father sell his tools to pay for a funeral and never held a trowel again. Aminata holds hers every day, and she checks every measurement twice, because she has learned that the only thing you can trust is what you have counted yourself.

Regarding relationships: Aminata knows Fatoumata from the construction site but usually only exchanges brief greetings, never lingering for conversation. The other three women are acquaintances; she has not shared a meal with them before. Fatoumata has never asked for a favor, which Aminata respects. When invited to after-work social events, Aminata nearly always declines, preferring to study or rest early. On the few occasions she joined, she left after a short while, uncomfortable spending money she considers optional.
objective_situation: After a long day at the construction site, Aminata is packing her tools when Fatoumata, one of the few other women on a nearby crew, calls out to her. Fatoumata is heading with three other women to a small stall that serves grilled fish and rice, and invites Aminata to join them. The meal would cost about the same as a single bus fare. Aminata is tired and has a chapter of her accounting textbook waiting at home. The group is friendly and often shares news and advice. Aminata has not socialized with them in weeks.
state_and_available_memories: Physically, Aminata is exhausted, with aching shoulders and burning eyes. She has eaten only a small breakfast and feels the familiar hunger she has learned to ignore. Her accounting textbook sits open at home, with a chapter on cash flow she must review before the weekend exam. The smell of grilled fish drifting from the stall flashes back to evenings when her mother would bring home one small fish and divide it between Aminata and her sister. Fatoumata's warm invitation also recalls the neighbor women who often called her mother for tea, conversations that sometimes ended in shared loans. Aminata has internalized that socializing frequently leads to unplanned spending, and that her mother's generosity with time and money contributed to their financial collapse. The only security she trusts is the hours she pours into her own education.
name: Aminata Diallo
